desc:
For two start positions i and j in s, the common extension is the length of the longest common prefix of the two suffixes s[i..] and s[j..]. In other words: how far can you read both suffixes simultaneously before the characters differ or one of the suffixes ends?

Each query is [i, j]. Return the common extension of every query, in order. If i = j, the answer is simply the length of the suffix n - i.

s = "abracadabra"
queries = [[0,7],[3,5],[1,8],[2,2]]
result  = [4,1,3,9]
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Walking along both suffixes until they differ is correct, but a highly repetitive string such as "ababab..." makes every query cost O(n).
If the two suffixes agree on their first L characters, they also agree on the first L - 1. That monotonic property allows a binary search on the answer.
Precompute prefix hashes of s. For a query, binary search the largest L ≤ n - max(i, j) for which the hashes of s[i..i+L) and s[j..j+L) are equal.
editorial: The predicate 'the first L characters of both suffixes agree' is true for L = 0, stays true up to the answer, and is false afterwards, so the answer is found by binary search over 0 .. n - max(i, j). Each predicate evaluation must be O(1): compare the polynomial hashes of the two blocks, computed from prefix hashes as H[a+L] - H[a] * B^L modulo a large prime.

Preprocessing takes O(n) and each query O(log n), for O(n + q log n) in total. The naive approach is O(q · n) in the worst case. A suffix array with an LCP array and a range-minimum structure answers each query in O(1) after an O(n log n) build, but the hashing solution is much shorter and fast enough here. Handle i = j separately or let the binary search cap it at n - i.
